title: Research
text:
My research focuses on using numerical models and machine learning methods to better understand complex physical processes like how glaciers flow or fires spread over the landscape. Much of my work has focused on glaciology, particularly looking at how glaciers and ice sheets respond to changes in climate.

Selected publications


[1] L. Zeller, D. McGrath, L. Sass, C. Florentine, and J. Downs, “Equilibrium line altitudes, accumulation areas and the vulnerability of glaciers in alaska,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 71, p. e28, Jan. 2025, doi: 10.1017/jog.2024.65.


[2] A. A. Marcozzi, J. V. Johnson, R. A. Parsons, S. J. Flanary, C. A. Seielstad, and J. Z. Downs, “Application of LiDAR derived fuel cells to wildfire modeling at laboratory scale,” Fire, vol. 6, no. 10, p. 394, Oct. 2023, doi: 10.3390/fire6100394.


[3] J. Downs and J. V. Johnson, “A rapidly retreating, marine-terminating glacier’s modeled response to perturbations in basal traction,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 68, no. 271, pp. 891–900, Oct. 2022, doi: 10.1017/jog.2022.5.


[4] J. P. Briner et al., “Rate of mass loss from the greenland ice sheet will exceed holocene values this century,” Nature, vol. 586, no. 7827, pp. 70–74, Oct. 2020, doi: 10.1038/s41586-020-2742-6.


[5] J. Z. Downs, J. V. Johnson, J. T. Harper, T. Meierbachtol, and M. A. Werder, “Dynamic hydraulic conductivity reconciles mismatch between modeled and observed winter subglacial water pressure,” Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, vol. 123, no. 4, pp. 818–836, 2018, doi: 10.1002/2017JF004522.


[6] B. D. Fleurian et al., “SHMIP the subglacial hydrology model intercomparison project,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 64, no. 248, pp. 897–916, Dec. 2018, doi: 10.1017/jog.2018.78.


[7] J. Downs, D. Brinkerhoff, and M. Morlighem, “Inferring time-dependent calving dynamics at helheim glacier,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 69, no. 274, pp. 381–396, Apr. 2023, doi: 10.1017/jog.2022.68.


[8] J. Downs, J. Johnson, J. Briner, N. Young, A. Lesnek, and J. Cuzzone, “Western greenland ice sheet retreat history reveals elevated precipitation during the holocene thermal maximum,” The Cryosphere, vol. 14, no. 3, pp. 1121–1137, Mar. 2020, doi: 10.5194/tc-14-1121-2020.

title: WARP.md
text:
This file provides guidance to WARP (warp.dev) when working with code in this repository.


This is an academic portfolio website built with Quarto and hosted on GitHub Pages. It contains research publications, teaching materials, blog posts, and personal information for Jacob Downs, an assistant professor at the University of Montana.






Root level: Main pages (index, research, teaching, about) as .qmd files
posts/: Blog posts and writing, with each post as a dated .qmd file

_metadata.yml: Default formatting configuration for all posts
index.qmd: Auto-generates listing page from post contents

**_site/**: Generated static site output (gitignored, do not edit directly)
images/: Static image assets referenced in content
**_quarto.yml**: Global site configuration (navigation, theme, bibliography)
references.bib: BibTeX bibliography for academic citations
styles.css: Custom CSS overrides




The site uses Quarto’s website project type with: - Theme: Cosmo (Bootstrap-based) - Citations: IEEE style via CSL, referencing references.bib - Navigation: Top navbar with Home, Research, Teaching, Writing, About - Output: HTML with right-side TOC and smooth scrolling



Automated via GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/publish.yml): 1. Triggers on push to main branch 2. Sets up Quarto environment 3. Runs quarto render to build _site/ 4. Deploys to GitHub Pages






# Render the entire site (generates _site/)
quarto render

# Preview site with live reload (opens browser at http://localhost:4200)
quarto preview

# Render a single file
quarto render path/to/file.qmd






Create a new .qmd file in posts/ with naming: YYYY-MM-DD-title.qmd
Include frontmatter with at minimum:
---
title: "Post Title"
date: YYYY-MM-DD
categories: [category1, category2]
---
The post automatically appears in posts/index.qmd listing





Add BibTeX entry to references.bib
Reference in .qmd files using [@citation_key]
For nocite (show in bibliography without inline citation), use frontmatter:
nocite: |
  @citation_key1
  @citation_key2





# Check Quarto version
quarto --version

# Validate project configuration
quarto check

# Clean build artifacts
rm -rf _site/ .quarto/







All content pages use .qmd (Quarto Markdown) format
Frontmatter is YAML between --- delimiters
Posts must include title, date, and categories in frontmatter





Academic references stored in references.bib (BibTeX format)
Citation keys follow format: authorlastname_titleword_year
Use IEEE citation style (configured globally in _quarto.yml)





Store in images/ directory
Reference using relative paths: images/filename.ext
Use Quarto image syntax for captions: ![caption](path){options}






Do not manually edit _site/: This directory is auto-generated by quarto render
GitHub Actions handles deployment: No manual deployment steps needed after pushing to main
Quarto must be installed locally to build/preview the site (not present in current environment)
Bibliography changes: After editing references.bib, re-render affected pages to update citations
Post listing is automatic: The posts/index.qmd uses Quarto’s listing feature to auto-populate from post files

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text: This note derives a strong-conservation form of the enthalpy equation in terrain-following sigma coordinates. The key goal is to rewrite the thermodynamics in a form that is compatible with a finite-volume method (FVM) on a deforming ice column.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: Why Conservative Form Matters for FVM
text:
Why Conservative Form Matters for FVM
The finite-volume method is built around a simple balance law: the rate of change of a conserved quantity inside a control volume must equal the net flux through its boundary plus any source terms. In continuous form, that structure is
\[
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q.
\]
In a terrain-following sigma coordinate system,
\[
\sigma = \frac{z - b}{H},
\]
the computational grid stretches and shrinks as the ice thickness \(H\) evolves. If the enthalpy equation is solved in its usual advective form, the solver tracks the transport of specific enthalpy \(E\) but does not account for the changing physical volume of each cell. That creates a numerical mismatch: total energy can be created or destroyed when the ice thickens or thins.
To recover strict conservation, the natural finite-volume state variable is the depth-integrated enthalpy per unit area, \(HE\).

section: 7. Thermodynamic Boundary Conditions in Conservative Form
text:
7. Thermodynamic Boundary Conditions in Conservative Form
Because the state variable is now \(HE\), the physical boundary conditions must be applied directly to the vertical fluxes.

Upper Surface Face (\(\sigma = 1\))
The total vertical flux is \(F_\sigma = E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H}\frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}\). At the surface, this has two components:

Advective flux from accumulation. Using \(\omega_s = -\dot{a}\): \[
F_{\sigma, \text{surface}}^{\text{adv}} = E_{\text{surface}} \omega_s = -E_{\text{surface}} \dot{a}.
\] Accumulation injects both mass and enthalpy consistently into the top control volume.
Diffusive flux from thermal conduction. The standard Dirichlet condition (\(E_s\) prescribed) implicitly determines this flux: the solver computes the gradient between the prescribed surface value and the first interior node, and the resulting conductive flux enters the sub-surface control volume naturally through the diffusion stencil.



Lower Bed Face (\(\sigma = 0\))
In the advective formulation, the bed requires a Neumann condition for diffusion: \(-\frac{\kappa}{H} \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}\right)_{\sigma=0} = q_{\text{geo}} + q_{\text{fric}}\).
In conservative form, the total basal flux \(F_{\sigma, \text{bed}}\) automatically combines this diffusive contribution with the advective contribution from melting (\(E_b \omega_b = -E_b \dot{m}\)):
\[
F_{\sigma, \text{bed}} = -E_b \dot{m} + q_{\text{geo}} + q_{\text{fric}}.
\]
If basal melting occurs, the exact corresponding enthalpy leaves the system in the same mathematical step as the mass loss.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
Numerical Implications
For a finite-volume implementation, this formulation gives a few immediate benefits:

Internal fluxes telescope exactly, so flux leaving one cell is the same flux entering its neighbor.
The evolving cell thickness \(H\) is tied directly to the transported quantity, which improves consistency on a deforming mesh.
In the limit \(u = v = \omega = 0\), the equation reduces to
\[
\frac{\partial (HE)}{\partial t} = 0,
\]
so column energy is conserved even as the control volume changes.







Takeaway



If the mesh thickness evolves, a solver that advances \(E\) alone is not strictly conservative. Advancing \(HE\) instead makes the thermodynamics compatible with finite-volume mass conservation and yields boundary conditions that are naturally expressed as energy fluxes.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 1. The Cartesian Baseline and the “Flux Problem” in Sigma Space
text:
1. The Cartesian Baseline and the “Flux Problem” in Sigma Space
The finite-volume method is built around a simple balance law: the rate of change of a conserved quantity inside a control volume must equal the net flux crossing its boundaries plus any internal source terms.
In a rigid Cartesian coordinate system \((x, y, z)\), the physical volume of a grid cell is constant. Because ice is treated as incompressible (\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\)), the Cartesian enthalpy equation naturally exists in a strong conservative, flux-divergence form:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}_{\text{Cartesian}} = Q_{\text{Cartesian}}
\]
Here, the total flux vector \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{Cartesian}}\) combines both advective transport (energy carried by the moving ice) and diffusive transport (thermal conduction). Neglecting horizontal diffusion, this vector is:
\[
\mathbf{F}_{\text{Cartesian}} = \mathbf{v}E - \mathbf{q}_{\text{diff}} = \begin{bmatrix} uE \\ vE \\ wE - \kappa \frac{\partial E}{\partial z} \end{bmatrix}
\]
The source term \(Q_{\text{Cartesian}}\) contains only the true volumetric generation or destruction of heat strictly inside the cell—specifically, internal strain heating (\(\Phi\)) and meltwater drainage:
\[
Q_{\text{Cartesian}} = \frac{\Phi}{\rho} - \frac{\rho_w}{\rho} L \, r_d \, \varpi(E)
\]
(where \(\kappa\) is the effective thermal diffusivity, \(\rho\) is ice density, and \(\varpi\) is the water content).
However, in a terrain-following sigma coordinate system,
\[
\sigma = \frac{z - b}{H},
\]
the computational grid stretches and shrinks over time as the ice thickness \(H\) evolves. If the enthalpy equation is transformed directly into its advective form, we get:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}
+ u \frac{\partial E}{\partial x}
+ v \frac{\partial E}{\partial y}
+ \dot{\sigma} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
= \frac{\partial q_{\text{diff}, \sigma}}{\partial \sigma} + Q_{\sigma}
\]
This creates a severe numerical issue for FVM. While the spatial terms (\(u \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} + \dots\)) represent advective transport (\(\mathbf{v}_\sigma \cdot \nabla_\sigma E\)), they cannot be trivially rewritten as a flux divergence (\(\nabla_\sigma \cdot (\mathbf{v}_\sigma E)\)). In Cartesian space, we could pull the velocity inside the derivative because the velocity field is divergenceless. In sigma space, the effective “velocity” field \((u, v, \dot{\sigma})\) is not divergenceless because the physical grid is deforming over time and space.
Because the equation cannot be natively forced into a divergence form, you cannot apply the Divergence Theorem to calculate an exact boundary flux. If an FVM solver updates \(E\) using these advective terms while the mass-continuity solver independently shrinks the cell thickness \(H\), total energy is numerically destroyed.
To recover strict conservation, we must force the equation back into a flux-divergence form by shifting the state variable from specific enthalpy \(E\) to the depth-integrated enthalpy per unit area, \(HE\).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
2. Governing Continuous Equations
To synthesize the conservative form, we must couple the thermodynamics with mass conservation.

The Vertical Diffusion Flux
To transform the Cartesian vertical diffusion \(\frac{\partial}{\partial z} (\kappa \frac{\partial E}{\partial z})\) into sigma coordinates, we apply the chain rule (\(\frac{\partial}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{H}\frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma}\)). Applying this to both the outer derivative and the inner gradient yields the sigma-space vertical diffusion divergence:
\[
\frac{\partial q_{\text{diff}, \sigma}}{\partial \sigma} = \frac{1}{H} \frac{\partial}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\kappa}{H} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma} \right)
\]


The Volumetric Source Term (\(Q\))
The internal source term \(Q\) remains identical in structure to its Cartesian counterpart, but its variables are now evaluated on the sigma grid:
\[
Q_{\sigma} = \frac{\Phi}{\rho} - \frac{\rho_w}{\rho} L \, r_d \, \varpi(E)
\]
The drainage term removes enthalpy from temperate ice to represent the gravitational percolation of liquid water out of the ice matrix (Aschwanden et al., 2012). The water content \(\varpi\) is defined as the liquid fraction above the pressure melting point (\(E_{\text{pmp}}\)):
\[
\varpi(E) = \frac{\max(E - E_{\text{pmp}}, \; 0)}{L}
\]
where \(E_{\text{pmp}} = c_i(T_{\text{pmp}} - T_{\text{ref}})\) is the enthalpy at the pressure melting point (which depends on the local overburden pressure via the Clausius-Clapeyron relation), \(L\) is the latent heat of fusion, and \(r_d\) is the drainage rate (units s\(^{-1}\)). Without this sink, temperate ice would accumulate unbounded water content — a physically unrealistic state that also degrades solver stability.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
Defining the FVM Face Fluxes
To implement this in a finite-volume solver, the equation must be expressed exactly as \(\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q\).
Because we unpacked \(S\) early on, we can explicitly separate the boundary-crossing transport terms (diffusion) from the purely internal generation terms (strain heating). By pulling the vertical diffusion component of \(HS\) over to the left-hand side, we define the complete total flux vector \(\mathbf{F}\) for the computational cell:
\[
\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_\sigma \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
HEu \\
HEv \\
E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The only remaining volumetric source term \(Q\) on the right-hand side is internal heat generation: \[
Q = \frac{H\Phi}{\rho}
\]

section: 8. Conclusion: Why This is the Desired FVM Form
text:
8. Conclusion: Why This is the Desired FVM Form
We began this derivation by noting that a finite-volume solver requires the governing equation to take a strict flux-divergence form:
\[
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q_{\text{total}}
\]
The equation we have derived satisfies this requirement in the computational space \((x, y, \sigma)\):

The Conserved Variable (\(U\)): The state variable tracked by the solver is \(U = HE\).
The Total Flux Vector (\(\mathbf{F}\)): Every spatial derivative now wraps entirely around a boundary-crossing flux (combining advection and diffusion): \[
\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_\sigma \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
HEu \\
HEv \\
E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The Internal Sources (\(Q_{\text{total}}\)): The remaining terms on the right-hand side are strictly volumetric: \(Q_{\text{total}} = \frac{H\Phi}{\rho} - \frac{H\rho_w}{\rho} L \, r_d \, \varpi(E)\), representing strain heating and meltwater drainage.







Numerical Payoff



By moving the grid thickness \(H\) inside the derivatives, the computational grid \((\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta \sigma)\) becomes completely static from the perspective of the FVM solver. The Divergence Theorem can now be safely applied.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
3. Transforming the Continuity Equation
To derive the conservative form, we must first map the Cartesian continuity equation into sigma space. We start with the Cartesian statement of incompressibility:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_z
+ \left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_z
+ \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}
= 0.
\]
When we change variables from \((x, y, z, t)\) to \((x, y, \sigma, t)\) where \(\sigma = \frac{z-b}{H}\), a horizontal derivative taken at a constant Cartesian depth \(z\) must account for the crossing of sloped \(\sigma\) layers. Applying the multivariate chain rule gives:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma + \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial x} \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma}
\] \[
\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma + \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial y} \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma}
\]
By applying the quotient rule to \(\sigma = \frac{z-b}{H}\), we explicitly evaluate the geometric derivatives:
\[
\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial x} = -\frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right), \qquad \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial y} = -\frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right), \qquad \frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{H}
\]
Substituting these into the chain rule expansions, our Cartesian continuity equation becomes:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} + \left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} + \frac{1}{H} \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} = 0
\]
To clear the fractions, we multiply the entire expression by the ice thickness \(H\):
\[
H\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma + H\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma + \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) = 0
\]
We want to force the horizontal terms into a flux-divergence form. Using the reverse product rule, we know that \(H\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x} - u\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}\). If we apply this to both horizontal velocities and manually add/subtract the time derivative \(\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}\) to complete the mass conservation statement, we can regroup the entire equation into two distinct brackets:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{ \left[ \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y} \right] }_{\text{Divergence of Horizontal Mass}} &+ \\
\underbrace{ \left[ \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) - \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) \right] }_{\text{Geometric Residuals}} &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 4. The Emergence of Relative Vertical Velocity (\(\omega\))
text:
4. The Emergence of Relative Vertical Velocity (\(\omega\))
The algebraic transformation leaves us with a clean horizontal divergence, but a massive residual of vertical and geometric cross-terms.
However, if we look closely at that second bracket, it is perfectly integrable with respect to \(\sigma\). We can define a new variable, \(\omega\), such that its vertical derivative \(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}\) is exactly equal to that entire second bracket:
\[
\omega = w - \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} \right) - \sigma \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right)
\]
(You can verify this by differentiating \(\omega\) with respect to \(\sigma\); because \(b\) and \(H\) do not depend on \(\sigma\), the differentiation exactly recovers the residual bracket).
By making this substitution, the messy transformed continuity equation collapses into the elegant sigma-space continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}
+ \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x}
+ \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y}
+ \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}
= 0.
\]
Physical Interpretation: While \(\omega\) emerged purely as a mathematical necessity to absorb the geometric residuals of the coordinate transformation, it has a strict physical meaning. It represents the scaled vertical velocity of the ice relative to the deforming computational grid. It takes the absolute vertical velocity (\(w\)) and subtracts the vertical motion caused by sliding along the bed (the first parenthetical) and the vertical motion caused by the stretching of the ice column (the second parenthetical).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
4. Transforming the Continuity Equation
With the geometry derivatives defined, we can now transform the Cartesian continuity equation into sigma space using the multivariate chain rule.
A horizontal derivative taken at a constant Cartesian depth \(z\) must account for the crossing of sloped \(\sigma\) layers:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma}
\]
\[
\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma}
\]
The vertical derivative transforms simply as \(\frac{\partial w}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{H} \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma}\).
Substituting these into the Cartesian continuity equation and multiplying the entire expression by the ice thickness \(H\) to clear fractions yields:
\[
H\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma + H\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma + \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) = 0
\]
To simplify this messy expression, we take the vertical derivative of our relative velocity equation (\(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}\)). Because \(b\) and \(H\) do not depend on \(\sigma\), this derivative isolates the exact geometric cross-terms seen above:
\[
\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) - \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right)
\]
Substituting this relationship back into our expanded continuity equation creates a massive cancellation, yielding the clean sigma-space continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}
+ \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x}
+ \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y}
+ \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}
= 0.
\]
